prerequisites: Good preparation on basic knowledge: order relation and algebra of real numbers, algebra of polynomials, elements of analytic geometry, elements of goniometry and trigonometry (solving a right triangle, Carnot's theorem and law of sines), elementary functions and their inverses or partial inverses (domain, codomain, graph; invertibility and monotonicity), function transformations (translations and scaling) and their effect on the graph, elementary equations and inequalities, systems of inequalities, elements of propositional logic (AND, OR, NOT conjunctions, De Morgan's laws).
Learning to learn: organize one's learning using various sources and information methods.

Communicate: understand and use messages of different types (mainly technical, scientific) and complexity, transmitted using different languages (natural, mathematical, symbolic, etc.) through different media (paper, computer, and multimedia).

learning_outcomes.text: Provide fundamental knowledge in the following areas: differential and integral calculus for functions of one variable, polynomial approximation, approximate solution of equations (both numerical and differential), data processing and elaboration, numerical integration, mathematical modeling with elementary tools (both discrete and continuous models).
Understand the fundamental role of infinitesimal and numerical calculus in modeling real phenomena and/or situations.
Basic competence in: understanding and conscious use of known mathematical models for describing phenomena or solving problems in real situations.
Basic competence in: constructing simple mathematical models for describing phenomena or solving problems in real situations.

Basic competence in: knowledge of the main structures of argumentative and demonstrative procedures in mathematical analysis, also through mastery of logical-formal language and its use in identifying and solving problems of various kinds.
Familiarity with the two key concepts of optimization and equilibrium and their applications in various fields, mainly industrial.

syllabus_topics: Study of dynamic evolution (sup/inf, limits, continuity, derivative)
Conservative maps (zeros theorem and Weierstrass theorem)
Zeros of a function: existence, uniqueness, localization of solutions, approximation algorithms (bisection; linearization methods: regula falsi, secant, Newton-Raphson)
Data fitting (polynomial interpolation and by splines; linear regression)
From discrete to continuous dynamic models
Existence, uniqueness, calculation of solutions (separable variables, homogeneous, linear)
Approximate solutions: epsilon-solution method, one-step algorithms (Euler, modified Euler)
Convergence criteria (ratio, Leibnitz, absolute convergence criteria)
teaching_methods: Lectures in the classroom for all course topics
Two written exercises in the classroom simulating the written exam
assessment_rules: The exam consists of a written test and an oral interview. The written test is divided into two consecutive phases, A and B. Phase A involves solving open-ended problems, with the use of handouts, manuals, and strictly offline graphic-symbolic calculation tools allowed. Phase B involves open-ended questions, with no paper or electronic support allowed. The oral interview assesses communication skills, language proficiency, and the ability to organize content exposition. The final grade is based on the results of both the written test and the oral interview.
